title: Make mercy your mosque
hook: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an (Majh ki Var M1, ang 140)

segments.voice: Yesterday, pitaa: the One as father, mother, kin and brother, so what fear can touch? Today Guru Nanak speaks to Muslim listeners in the words of their own faith.

Guru Nanak spent his life among both Muslims and Hindus. Tradition remembers his companion on the road, Bhai Mardana, as a Muslim musician who played the rabab beside him. In the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak often speaks to people in the language of their own practice. To Hindus he talks about the sacred thread, the pilgrimage, the lamp. To Muslims, the mosque, the prayer mat, the fast. And in one salok in Majh ki Var, he builds a whole mosque without a single brick.
screen: `AMONG MUSLIMS AND HINDUS.` → `IN THE LANGUAGE OF THEIR PRACTICE.` → `A MOSQUE WITHOUT A BRICK.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 140. It goes, in effect: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, and what is honest and rightfully earned your Qur'an. Make modesty and good conduct your observances and your fast; so become a Muslim. Make good deeds your Kaaba, truth your guide, and good works your creed and your prayer. Let your rosary be whatever pleases Him. Then, Nanak, He will keep your honor. The word for mercy is mihar: kindness, compassion. It would be easy to hear this wrongly, as Guru Nanak telling Muslims to give up their mosques. That's not what the text says. He doesn't ask anyone to stop praying, fasting or going to the mosque. He asks what all of it is for, and answers: mercy, faith, honest living, truth, good deeds. It's the same move he makes toward Hindus in Asa di Var, describing a sacred thread spun from compassion and contentment. In both, he speaks from inside the listener's own words. For Sikhs, the question turns right back on themselves. What makes a gurdwara a gurdwara? What is the turban for, the Ardas, the langar? Read that way, the salok's question fits every house of worship, a gurdwara included. A person can kneel on the finest prayer mat in the world, or bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, and still need to ask whether mercy came in with them.
screen: `MIHAR: MERCY, COMPASSION.` · `MERCY THE MOSQUE, FAITH THE MAT.` · `NOT GIVING IT UP: FILLING IT.` · `THE QUESTION TURNS BACK ON SIKHS.` · then, large: `MERCY IS THE MOSQUE.`

segments.voice: Picture walking into the place where you pray, rest or find quiet, a mosque, a gurdwara, a church, a bench by a lake, your own bedroom, and ask Guru Nanak's question: did mercy come in with me? Then think of one small, real merciful act: a patient answer, a meal shared, a debt forgiven, a kind word to someone struggling. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and hold that act before the One.
Mihar, mercy, kindness: Guru Nanak, speaking in Islam's own words, makes it the mosque, faith the prayer mat, honest living the Qur'an.
Your line: mercy is the mosque. What is all of it for? That's day six hundred fifty-four.

screen: `DAY 654 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YOU SPENT THE NIGHT SLEEPING.`

howItsDone: Sikhs sing and recite Majh ki Var in the gurdwara, and often cite this salok of Guru Nanak as teaching that every outward practice is fulfilled through mercy, faith and honest living.

what a scholar hears: the salok maps virtues onto Islamic institutions point by point (maseet, musallaa, Qur'an, rozaa, Kaaba, kalmaa, nivaaj, tasbee), as Asa di Var does for the Hindu janeu; both can be read as addressed to everyone, Sikhs included.

chat.says: In that salok, is Guru Nanak telling Muslims to stop going to the mosque?
options: No: he asks what it's all for, mercy, faith, honest living, in Islam's own words.
Yes, he says real faith needs no mosque, no fast and no prayer at all.
He's asking Muslims to become Sikhs and pray in a gurdwara instead.
chat.meaning: The salok doesn't ask anyone to stop praying or fasting; it asks what it's all for: mercy, faith, honest living, truth and good deeds.
